Sheet resistance target: 100-150 ohm/sq for a lightly doped emitter (low Auger recombination, high Voc) when combined with fine-line metallization. The emitter profile (surface concentration, junction depth) is a trade-off: heavier doping reduces contact resistance but increases Auger recombination and reduces blue response.

Design surface passivation. Front: SiO2/SiNx stack (the thin SiO2 from thermal oxidation provides excellent chemical passivation, the SiNx provides field-effect passivation with fixed positive charge and hydrogen). Rear for TOPCon: thin tunnel SiO2 (1.5 nm by chemical oxidation or thermal) plus doped polysilicon (n+ poly-Si, 100-200nm, phosphorus-doped). The tunnel oxide allows majority carrier transport while blocking minority carrier recombination. Target interface recombination current J0 < 5 fA/cm^2 for the passivated contact.

Validate passivation quality. Measure implied Voc (iVoc) and effective minority carrier lifetime by photoconductance decay (Sinton WCT-120). Target iVoc > 720 mV for TOPCon. Measure J0 by the Kane-Swanson method (lifetime at multiple injection levels). Map spatially using photoluminescence imaging to identify passivation non-uniformity before metallization.

steps.description: Design the metallization pattern and integrate the cell into a module with appropriate encapsulation for 25-year reliability.

inputs.name: cell-architecture
inputs.desc: Cell structure and contact requirements

inputs.name: junction-formation-recipe
inputs.desc: Emitter sheet resistance determining contact difficulty

inputs.name: efficiency-loss-budget
inputs.desc: Allowable grid shading and series resistance losses

outputs.name: metallization-design
outputs.desc: Grid pattern, finger width, busbar design, and paste selection

outputs.name: module-design
outputs.desc: Cell-to-module assembly, encapsulant, backsheet, and frame specification

outputs.name: reliability-qualification-plan
outputs.desc: IEC 61215 test sequence and expected degradation

process: Design the front grid pattern. Finger width is limited by screen printing (currently 25-35 um for fine-line). Finger spacing optimizes the trade-off: closer spacing reduces resistive loss in the emitter (current travels less distance laterally) but increases shading loss. The optimal spacing: d = sqrt(2 * rho_sheet * w_finger / (J_sc * R_finger)) where rho_sheet is emitter sheet resistance, w_finger is printed width, J_sc is short-circuit current density, R_finger is finger line resistance per length. Multi-busbar (MBB) with 9-16 round wires reduces both bubar shading and finger length.

Select the metallization paste. Front: silver paste for contact to the emitter (must fire through the SiNx ARC at 750-800C peak firing temperature). Contact resistance target: < 1 mOhm*cm^2. For TOPCon rear: silver or silver-aluminum paste contacting the doped polysilicon. Paste cost is significant (silver at $1000/kg, 50-100 mg per cell). Copper plating is an alternative (lower cost, finer lines, lower resistance) but requires a seed layer and plating equipment.

Fire the metallization. Co-firing in a belt furnace with a carefully profiled temperature ramp: 1) burnout zone (400-500C, organic binders removed), 2) firing zone (750-800C peak for 1-3 seconds, silver frit etches through ARC and forms contact to silicon), 3) rapid cooling. The peak temperature window is narrow: too low gives poor contact, too high causes aluminum spiking or junction shunting. In-line process monitoring by Suns-Voc and IV testing.

Design the module. Cell stringing (half-cut cells reduce resistive loss by 75% vs full cells). Encapsulant: EVA (mainstream, yellows slightly over 25 years) or POE (better moisture barrier, less PID susceptibility). Front glass: 3.2mm tempered with AR coating. Backsheet: fluoropolymer or glass-glass for bifacial. Frame: anodized aluminum for mechanical protection and mounting. Junction box with bypass diodes (1 per substring of 20-24 cells) for hot spot protection.

Qualify for IEC 61215. Key tests: thermal cycling (TC200: 200 cycles from -40C to +85C), damp heat (DH1000: 1000 hours at 85C/85%RH), UV exposure, mechanical load (5400 Pa front, 2400 Pa rear), hail impact (25mm ice ball at 23 m/s). Pass criterion: < 5% power degradation after each test. PID (potential-induced degradation) test: 1000V system voltage at 85C/85%RH for 96 hours. Predict field degradation: 0.3-0.5%/year for crystalline silicon modules, warranted to 80% of nameplate at 25-30 years.

description: Design the fundamental systems of a particle accelerator from beam dynamics through RF cavities, magnets, vacuum, and diagnostics.

steps.description: Design the beam optics lattice and calculate the key beam parameters for the target energy and luminosity.

inputs.name: beam-energy-target
inputs.desc: Target particle energy and species (electrons, protons, heavy ions)

inputs.name: beam-current-luminosity
inputs.desc: Target beam current or luminosity for the physics program

inputs.name: accelerator-type
inputs.desc: Linac, synchrotron, storage ring, or fixed-field alternating gradient

outputs.name: lattice-design
outputs.desc: Magnet arrangement (FODO cells, chicanes, insertion regions) with Twiss parameters

outputs.name: beam-parameters
outputs.desc: Emittance, beta functions, beam size, and energy spread

outputs.name: rf-requirements
outputs.desc: RF frequency, voltage, and harmonic number from the lattice circumference

process: Design the basic lattice cell. The FODO cell (focusing-drift-defocusing-drift) is the standard building block. Quadrupole strengths set the betatron tune (number of oscillations per revolution): Q_x and Q_y must avoid resonance conditions (not near integer, half-integer, or low-order fractions). Phase advance per cell of 60-90 degrees is typical. The maximum beta function in the cell determines the required magnet aperture.

Calculate beam size from emittance and beta function: sigma = sqrt(epsilon * beta) where epsilon is the geometric emittance (invariant for protons if no radiation, decreasing with energy for electrons due to synchrotron radiation). For a proton synchrotron, normalized emittance epsilon_n = beta_rel * gamma * epsilon is conserved. For an electron ring, equilibrium emittance is set by the balance of quantum excitation and radiation damping.

Design insertion regions. Interaction points (for colliders) need low-beta insertions to squeeze the beam to small size (high luminosity: L = N1*N2*f*gamma / (4*pi*sigma_x*sigma_y)). The final focus triplet provides the squeeze but generates high beta at the triplet (chromatic aberration). Injection and extraction regions need kicker magnets with fast rise time and septum magnets for beam separation.

Determine RF parameters. RF frequency: h * f_rev where h is the harmonic number (number of buckets) and f_rev is the revolution frequency. The RF voltage must provide sufficient bucket area for the beam energy spread: V_rf = 2*pi*h*eta*delta_E / (q*cos(phi_s)) where eta is the slip factor, delta_E is the energy spread, and phi_s is the synchronous phase. For acceleration, phi_s shifts from 0 to provide net energy gain per turn.

Analyze collective effects. Space charge tune shift: delta_Q = -N*r_p / (4*pi*epsilon_n*beta^2*gamma^3*B_f) where N is particles per bunch, r_p is classical proton radius, B_f is the bunching factor. This limits intensity in low-energy rings. Impedance-driven instabilities (resistive wall, beam-beam) set current limits at high energy. Simulate with tracking codes (MAD-X for optics, elegant for tracking with collective effects).

steps.description: Design the RF acceleration system from frequency and voltage requirements through cavity geometry, power source, and control.

inputs.name: rf-requirements
inputs.desc: Frequency, voltage, and power from beam dynamics

inputs.name: beam-energy-target
inputs.desc: Energy gain per pass or turn

inputs.name: accelerator-type
inputs.desc: Linac (single-pass) vs ring (multi-pass)

outputs.name: cavity-design
outputs.desc: Cavity geometry, material, operating mode, and Q factor

outputs.name: rf-power-source
outputs.desc: Klystron, IOT, or solid-state amplifier specification

outputs.name: rf-control-system
outputs.desc: Low-level RF feedback for amplitude and phase stability

process: Select cavity technology. Normal-conducting copper cavities: simple, moderate Q (10,000-50,000), limited by wall losses (surface resistance scales as sqrt(f)), suitable for low duty cycle (pulsed linacs) or lower frequency (cyclotrons). Superconducting niobium cavities: high Q (1e9 to 1e11), much lower wall power but require cryogenic cooling (2K or 4K), standard for CW and high-duty-cycle machines (e.g., LCLS-II, ESS, LHC).

Design the cavity geometry. The fundamental mode (TM010 for a pillbox) gives an accelerating electric field along the axis. The shunt impedance R/Q (a geometry-only figure of merit) determines the voltage per unit stored energy. Elliptical cavities (TESLA/ILC shape) have R/Q ~ 1000 ohm at 1.3 GHz, with optimized cell shape to minimize peak surface fields (Epk/Eacc < 2, Bpk/Eacc < 4 mT/(MV/m)) to avoid field emission and quench.

Calculate the required RF power. For a superconducting cavity: P_beam = V_acc * I_beam (beam loading), P_wall = V_acc^2 / (R/Q * Q0) (cavity wall dissipation, small for SRF). Total RF power includes beam loading, wall losses, and power reflected due to detuning. The coupling factor (Q_ext) is set to match: Q_ext = Q0 at zero beam loading, or Q_ext = V_acc^2 / (R/Q * P_beam) for heavy beam loading.

Select the RF power source. Klystron: high power (hundreds of kW to MW), efficient at narrow bandwidth, standard for large accelerators. IOT (inductive output tube): better efficiency at lower power, used for storage rings. Solid-state amplifiers: modular, redundant, lower power per unit but scalable, increasingly used for new facilities. Match the source bandwidth and power to the cavity requirement including Lorentz force detuning compensation.

Design the low-level RF (LLRF) control. Feedback loops stabilize the cavity field amplitude (to 0.01% for FEL-quality beams) and phase (to 0.01 degrees). The control bandwidth must be faster than the dominant perturbation (microphonics at 1-100 Hz for SRF, beam transients at revolution frequency). Digital LLRF systems sample at tens of MHz, apply IQ demodulation, and compute correction signals in an FPGA. Feedforward for known perturbations (Lorentz detuning, beam loading) plus feedback for unknown disturbances.

steps.description: Design the magnet system, vacuum system, and beam diagnostics for reliable accelerator operation.

inputs.name: lattice-design
inputs.desc: Magnet positions, strengths, and aperture requirements

inputs.name: beam-parameters
inputs.desc: Beam size, current, and energy

inputs.name: beam-energy-target
inputs.desc: Maximum beam rigidity (B*rho = p/q)

outputs.name: magnet-specifications
outputs.desc: Dipole and quadrupole designs with field quality requirements

outputs.name: vacuum-system-design
outputs.desc: Beam pipe material, pumping scheme, and target pressure

outputs.name: diagnostics-suite
outputs.desc: BPM, beam profile, current, and loss monitor specifications

process: Design dipole magnets. For a given beam rigidity B*rho = p/(q*c), the bending radius is rho = B*rho / B. Higher field means smaller radius and smaller machine. Normal conducting iron-core magnets: up to 1.8T. Superconducting NbTi at 4.2K: up to 8-9T (LHC). Nb3Sn at 4.5K: up to 12-16T (HL-LHC upgrade). HTS (REBCO): potentially 20T+, under development. Field quality requirement: field homogeneity better than 1e-4 over the good field region (beam aperture) to avoid resonance driving terms.

Design quadrupole magnets. The gradient G = d^2B/dx^2 is specified by the lattice design. Aperture = beam pipe diameter + alignment tolerance + good field region margin. For superconducting quadrupoles, the gradient is limited by the conductor at the pole tip: B_pole = G * r_aperture. Iron saturation limits normal-conducting quadrupoles to about 20 T/m at 50mm aperture. Field quality multipoles (sextupole, octupole) must be below 1e-4 of the main quadrupole at the reference radius.

Design the vacuum system. For electron storage rings: synchrotron radiation desorbs gas from the beam pipe wall; the design pressure (1e-9 mbar) is achieved by distributed pumping (NEG coating on the inner beam pipe surface, plus discrete ion pumps). For proton rings: beam-induced electron cloud can cause pressure rise; mitigate with surface treatment (amorphous carbon coating, sawtooth chamber). Beam pipe material: stainless steel (standard), copper (for synchrotron radiation power), aluminum (reduced impedance, LHC). All-metal seals (Conflat) for UHV integrity.

Design beam position monitors (BPMs). Button or stripline pickups detect the beam image current. Four electrodes (top, bottom, left, right) give horizontal and vertical position from the difference-over-sum signal. Resolution of 1-10 um RMS is typical for modern digital BPM electronics. Orbit correction uses BPM data and corrector dipole magnets in a feedback loop (beam-based alignment, orbit response matrix inversion).

Design beam loss monitors. Ionization chambers or scintillator-PMT detectors around the ring detect particle losses. A machine protection system (MPS) uses loss monitor signals to trigger a beam dump if losses exceed safe thresholds (quench protection for superconducting magnets, or activation limits). Loss maps (measured loss pattern versus artificial orbit bump) verify the collimation system performance. The beam dump system must extract the full beam within one revolution for fast failures.
